activities.anchor: moved one more property of these worlds from speculation to measurement
activities.caption: rebuild the field's three dates
activities.name: exDatesOrder

config.prompt: Three dates moved exoplanets from nothing to thousands:
items: 1992: first confirmed exoplanets — two terrestrial bodies orbiting a pulsar, found by millisecond tick timing
1995: 51 Pegasi b — a Jupiter-mass planet on a 4.2-day orbit, found by radial velocity
2009: Kepler's transits multiply the census by thousands
config.why: Hot Jupiters were so unexpected that theorists had to invent planetary migration — giants forming far out and spiralling inward.

activities.anchor: a rock with a sky from a ball of hydrogen
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the dip arithmetic
activities.name: exDipSpot

config.prompt: One line of this transit answer is wrong — click it:
lines: A planet crossing its star blocks a flux fraction δ = (Rp/Rs)².
Jupiter blocking the Sun: (1/10)² = 1% — a 10,000-ppm dip, easily seen.
Earth blocking the Sun: (1/109)² ≈ 80 ppm — the number that sent Kepler to space.
A bigger planet makes a shallower dip, since the ratio squares.
config.correction: A bigger planet makes a DEEPER dip — δ grows with the square of the radius ratio.
config.why: The squared ratio is the whole method: Jupiter's 10,000-ppm dip is trivial; Earth's 80-ppm dip needed a space telescope.

config.prompt: The commonest planet type is the super-Earth/mini-Neptune class (1–4 Earth radii). Place the 'radius valley' — the scarcity boundary — on the scale (Earth radii):
config.why: The valley at ~1.8 R⊕ marks the boundary where planets keep or lose their hydrogen envelopes to photoevaporation.
config.context: TRAPPIST-1's seven Earth-sized worlds cycle in resonant clockwork 40 light-years away.

activities.caption: file the methods — what does each actually read?
activities.name: exMethodBuckets

config.prompt: No method sees the planet directly — each reads one shadow. File them:

items.label: direct imaging — coronagraph, young hot giants on wide orbits
radial velocity — a periodic Doppler shift of spectral lines
the transit — a repeating dip in starlight
microlensing — a sharp blip as a foreground star lenses a background one
pulsar timing — millisecond precision on a dead star's ticks

config.why: Each method samples different masses and orbits — the full picture only exists because they overlap.

config.q: The exoplanet images in the news — swirling disks, blue marbles, orbit diagrams — are…
choices: illustrations of data — almost every Earth-sized world is known from a dip, a wobble or a timing blip in a single point of starlight
config.why: Direct imaging has resolved only a few dozen young, self-luminous giants — which makes the atmospheres JWST has read out of those faint dips the more remarkable.

activities.caption: call the magnitude — Earth twins in the galaxy
activities.name: exTwinEstimate

config.prompt: Kepler's statistics put roughly one in five sun-like stars with an Earth-sized planet in its habitable zone. On that rate, roughly how many such worlds are in the Milky Way?
config.why: On the order of ten billion — and tens of billions counting red dwarfs.
config.context: The zone is necessary, never sufficient: Venus and Mars sit near the Sun's HZ edges, and both lost their shot.

activities.anchor: the atmospheres JWST has already read out of those faint dips
activities.caption: pair each world with its lesson
activities.name: exWorldMatch

config.prompt: The landmark worlds, each teaching one thing:

pairs.right: the first hot Jupiter — migration invented to explain it
resonant clockwork whose transit-timing variations revealed their masses
direct imaging's showcase — young, hot, self-luminous, wide
the galaxy's commonest planet — absent from our own system

config.why: And the radius valley at ~1.8 R⊕ marks where worlds keep or lose their hydrogen envelopes.
